name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Sunday 13 July 1986

clue.text: Stupors caused by mixing these small vegetables

indicators.note: mixing jumbles things together, so the word's letters come out in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Dazed states are blamed on tossing together some little vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: Brussels sprouts, usually just called sprouts, are small cabbage-like vegetables.

clue.text: Quivering sound from room to let, somehow

indicators.note: somehow means by some unstated method, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A trembling noise coming from a vacant room advertised for rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Room to let' reads as one phrase, a rental notice, but 'to' only joins the two words being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A tremolo is a wavering, trembling effect in music or the voice.

clue.text: Child's play to get young goat to eat greedily

blocks.note: a kid is a young goat
to stuff oneself is to gorge on food

explanation.surface: A goat kid wolfing down its food is presented as something childishly easy.
explanation.walkthrough: The page was scanned, and 'cat' is an OCR slip for 'eat'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kid stuff is an informal idiom for something trivially easy, the same as child's play.

clue.text: Royal Navy breaks into ships' bottoms — they're inside nuts

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the keel runs along the bottom of a ship
RN is the standard abbreviation for Royal Navy

explanation.surface: The navy smashes into the undersides of vessels, a nautical scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Kernels are the edible seeds found inside nutshells.

clue.text: It's barren to put 49 into a cubic foot

indicators.note: putting one thing into another places it inside

blocks.note: a stere is a unit of volume for firewood, strictly a cubic metre
49 in Roman numerals is written IL here, 50 less 1

explanation.surface: A dry numerical puzzle about fitting a number into a volume.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter loosely calls the stere a cubic foot; it is a cubic metre. Strictly, 49 is XLIX, but IL is a crossword shortcut.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterile describes land or living things that are unable to produce, so it means barren.

clue.text: Not cloyed from ingredients of sad tune

indicators.note: ingredients are mixed together in cooking, so these letters go into the pot and come out rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is not sickened by the makings of a mournful melody.
explanation.definitionFit: To cloy is to sicken with excess, so not cloyed means not satiated or filled up.

clue.text: Kind of leaf about the German, relating to Central Government

indicators.note: 'kind of' means a variety of the next word, so its letters appear in another arrangement
about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go around the next piece

blocks.note: der is German for 'the' with a masculine noun

explanation.surface: A botanical note about a leaf type and German connections to the state.
explanation.definitionFit: Federal refers to the national or central level of government in a federation such as Australia.

clue.text: Separates, and could be thinly spread when tea is removed

indicators.note: something removed is taken away, so those letters come out of the longer word
'could be' suggests the remaining letters may become something else when rearranged

blocks.note: the opening word, taken as written, supplies the letters
taken as written; these three letters are the ones to take out

explanation.surface: Someone notes that something which separates might end up spread thin once the tea is taken out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Separates' looks like the definition at the front, but it is the raw material: lose T, E and A and rearrange the six letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparse describes something scattered thinly, with few items over a wide area.

clue.text: Set free from housing contract in the red

indicators.note: housing means holding something inside, so one word sits within the other

blocks.note: taken as written; this is the outer word
a lease is a rental contract

explanation.surface: Someone is freed from a rental agreement while their finances are in the red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the red' suggests debt, but here 'in' just places the contract word within RED.
explanation.definitionFit: Released is a past participle meaning liberated or let go, matching set free.

clue.text: A conquest and not a fellow

explanation.surface: A tale of a conquest that involved no man at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: 'A conquest' points to the famous Norman Conquest of England in 1066.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norman Conquest is the best-known conquest in English history, so the clue treats the adjective as naming one.

clue.text: He joins up willingly — a kind of listener

indicators.note: 'a kind of' says the following word appears in another form, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written; all eight letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A volunteer recruit is described as a particular sort of good listener.
explanation.definitionFit: An enlister is one who enlists, signing up for military service by choice.

clue.text: Large stop signs contain legal bars

indicators.note: the words before it are said to contain the answer within their run of letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and through the next two

explanation.surface: Big stop signs are imagined as displaying courtroom prohibitions.
explanation.walkthrough: An estop is a legal bar: in law, estoppel stops a party from asserting something contrary to what they said earlier.
explanation.definitionFit: To estop is a legal term for preventing someone from making a claim, so estops are legal bars.

clue.text: I got set to disturb a self centred person

indicators.note: disturbing things throws them out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to unsettle a vain acquaintance.
explanation.definitionFit: An egotist is someone excessively absorbed in themselves and their own importance.

clue.text: Principal ocean?

blocks.note: surface reading: the chief or largest of the world's oceans
setter's reading: a word for principal that, with the article, is also an old poetic name for the open sea

explanation.walkthrough: Main means chief, and 'the main' is a literary term for the high seas, as in the Spanish Main.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an archaic, poetic expression for the open sea, while its second word alone means chief.

clue.text: Childish talk to rave on about trivial ends -

indicators.note: ends picks out the first and last letters of the word before it
about means around, so the verb's letters wrap the selected pair

blocks.note: to prate is to talk on foolishly at length
the first and last letters of trivial

explanation.surface: A complaint about babble that goes on and on over trivial matters.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash carries on into 14 Down, a common way to run one sentence across two clues; it is not part of either wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Prattle is foolish or childlike chatter.

clue.text: Fuel "Ad" demonstrating vassal relationship

indicators.note: the quotation marks and the 'demonstrating' that follows set the two words up to be worked into new order

explanation.surface: A fuel advertisement is said to show master and servant at work.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no strong anagram signal; the solver simply notices that the six letters of the first two words rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The feudal system bound vassals to lords, so feudal describes that relationship of service.

clue.text: - for kind of grey counterfeiting

indicators.note: 'kind of' signals a variant of the following word, so its letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Continuing from 13 Down: idle talk about a shade of grey being faked.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dash links this clue to the sentence begun in 13 Down; read on its own, it is complete.
explanation.definitionFit: Forgery is the crime of making fake copies, the same as counterfeiting.

clue.text: Rumba, for example, could produce sense of injury

indicators.note: 'could produce' suggests the letters can be made into something new by rearranging them

blocks.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for 'for example'

explanation.surface: A dance like the rumba might leave someone feeling hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For example' looks like it introduces the rumba as an example of a dance; it actually supplies two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Umbrage is offence or resentment, a feeling of having been slighted or wronged.

clue.text: Donkey, for example, has first-class spear

blocks.note: A1 means first-class, with the digit 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A donkey, say, is said to own a superb spear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Donkey, for example' reads as one idea, but it is two pieces. A1 is an old rating for first-class, and its 1 stands in for I.
explanation.definitionFit: An assegai is a slender iron-tipped spear used in southern Africa.

clue.text: Controller who could make poet roar

indicators.note: 'could make' suggests the letters can be turned into something else

explanation.surface: A person in control is credited with making a poet bellow.
explanation.definitionFit: An operator is someone who runs or controls a machine or system.

clue.text: Strangely dressed in a kind of red bag

indicators.note: 'a kind of' means a version of the following words, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone oddly turned out in some sort of red sack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strangely' looks like the anagram signal, but it belongs to the definition: garb suggests distinctive, often unusual clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Garbed means clothed, usually in a distinctive or unusual outfit.

clue.text: In Canberra I've become idle

blocks.note: Canberra lies in the ACT, the Australian Capital Territory

explanation.surface: A resident complains that life in the capital has made them lazy.
explanation.walkthrough: A local touch for the Canberra Times: ACT is the Australian Capital Territory, the territory that contains Canberra.
explanation.definitionFit: Inactive and idle are synonyms, both meaning not working or doing nothing.

clue.text: An overcoat type — some extra glances are merited

indicators.note: 'some' means only part of the following words is used, a run of their letters

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A particular style of coat is said to deserve a few second looks.
explanation.definitionFit: A raglan is a style of overcoat with sleeves running in one piece up to the collar, named after Lord Raglan.

clue.text: Incline to rely, in a way, in gentle manner

indicators.note: 'in a way' means after a fashion, so the word before it comes out in a different form

blocks.note: to tend is to incline or lean towards

explanation.surface: Advice to lean on someone, after a fashion, softly.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenderly is an adverb meaning with gentleness and care.
